solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pater's new woman? Pater spent freely!

indicators.note: used freely, the letters of the two words are spent loosely and rearranged

explanation.surface: A father has remarried, and his new partner is free with his money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'freely' rearranges the ten letters of PATER and SPENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A father's new wife becomes a step-mother to his children, one kind of stepparent.

clue.text: Rural area lacking river in Shropshire?

indicators.note: lacking means the following letter is dropped from the word for rural area

parts.note: rural area means the country

explanation.surface: A stretch of rural Shropshire has no river running through it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' removes R from COUNTRY. Shropshire is an English county, and the question mark flags it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Shropshire is an example of a British administrative shire, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Set off having big cheese to sell

parts.note: a big cheese is an important person, a star
to tout is to sell, especially tickets aggressively

explanation.surface: A celebrity is starting a business selling something.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off on a journey is to start out, a phrasal synonym.

clue.text: Spin bowler had briefly to be cautioned by umpire?

parts.note: Shane Warne was a famous Australian leg-spin bowler
had is shortened to 'd, as in I'd

explanation.surface: A spin bowler gets a formal caution from the cricket umpire.
explanation.walkthrough: Shane Warne was a great Australian spin bowler in cricket; an umpire may give a player an official caution.
explanation.definitionFit: An umpire gives formal cautions, so a cricketer told off has been officially admonished.

clue.text: Opponent with weapon trapping a West Indian

parts.note: an anti is someone opposed to something

indicators.note: trapping means the weapon closes around the following letter

parts.note: a gun is a weapon

explanation.surface: An armed adversary has captured a man from the Caribbean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trapping' signals the container; 'with' just joins the two parts. Antigua is a Caribbean island.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Antigua, an island in the Caribbean, is a West Indian.

clue.text: Escape with payment, having pocketed pounds

indicators.note: having pocketed means the payment word holds the next letter inside

parts.note: a fee is a payment
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A thief makes off with the money after pocketing the cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having pocketed' puts L inside FEE.
explanation.definitionFit: To flee is to run away, a direct verb synonym for escaping.

clue.text: Plays theatrically as cast maybe

parts.note: the word cast is the letters of acts made out of order

explanation.surface: Actors perform with exaggerated drama, as a theatre cast might.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read ACTS with OUT as an anagram signal, and the result is CAST. 'maybe' flags that indirection.
explanation.definitionFit: To play something out theatrically is to dramatise it, a phrasal synonym.

clue.text: Trying perhaps to look chic somehow or other?

definitions.meaning: read literally, chasing the latest style
in some rough way, not very well

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in a rough or imperfect way; read literally it means pursuing style.

clue.text: Type of creature destroyed by lindane

indicators.note: destroyed by means the letters of the insecticide name are wrecked and rearranged

explanation.surface: A kind of animal is wiped out by an insecticide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed by' rearranges LINDANE. Lindane is a pesticide, which makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: An annelid is a segmented worm such as an earthworm, one type of animal.

clue.text: Candid mister, I fancy, was biased

indicators.note: fancy as a verb of imagining, here a signal that the letters are rearranged fancifully

explanation.surface: An outspoken man admits he thinks something was prejudiced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' rearranges CANDID MISTER I. It looks like 'I suppose' in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To have discriminated against someone is to have treated them unfairly with prejudice.

clue.text: Game advice naughtily given to illegal dumpers?

definitions.meaning: a casual form of cricket where batters must run after hitting

definitions.text: advice naughtily given to illegal dumpers?
definitions.meaning: dump your rubbish and flee, as a fly-tipper might be told

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain to tip is to dump rubbish; fly-tipping is illegal dumping.
explanation.definitionFit: A casual cricket game shares its name with literal advice to dump rubbish and escape.

clue.text: Intestinal condition with release of some bile usually

indicators.note: release of some says letters are let out from the words that follow, a run hidden inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A gut complaint sometimes comes with the discharge of bile.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'with release' into the definition, but this condition is a blockage, not a release; 'release of some' is the hidden-word signal and 'with' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Ileus is a medical term for an obstruction of the intestine, a bowel condition.

clue.text: Willing to study, having the yen

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university
Y is the abbreviation for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: Someone keen to study has a yearning to learn.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ready to do something means being prepared and willing to do it.

clue.text: Three possibly dazed when taken in by stranger

indicators.note: taken in by means the dazed word is held inside the word for stranger

parts.note: stranger means more odd, odder
numb means dazed, without feeling

explanation.surface: Three people were stunned when a newcomer welcomed them in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in by' signals the container and 'when' links. 'Three' looks like a count of people but is the number itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Three is an example of an integer not divisible by two, hence 'possibly'.

clue.text: Person who's good with Latin, philosopher who may erect barriers

parts.note: a brick is an old-fashioned term for a reliable, good person
A. J. Ayer was a British philosopher

explanation.surface: A good Latin scholar and a philosopher may put up intellectual barriers.
explanation.walkthrough: Calling someone 'a brick' is dated British praise for a dependable person.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lays bricks builds walls, which are physical barriers.

clue.text: Bound to be seen in appropriate old cinema?

indicators.note: to be seen in means the word for bound sits inside the word for appropriate

parts.note: fit means appropriate or suitable
a bound is a jump, a leap

explanation.surface: Someone is sure to be spotted at a suitable old picture house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be seen in' signals the container. 'Bound' looks like 'certain' but is a jump. A fleapit is British slang for a shabby old cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleapit is a jokey British term for a run-down, dirty cinema, supposedly flea-infested.

clue.text: The sort of blubber you expect with an immature person

definitions.text: The sort of blubber you expect with an immature person

parts.words: The sort of blubber you expect with an immature person
parts.note: blubber read as body fat rather than crying: the plumpness a child or adolescent carries before slimming down

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the plumpness of a child or teenager, which usually disappears with growth.

clue.text: Authenticate name held by two companies

indicators.note: held by means the name letter is gripped inside the two company words

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
a firm is a company

explanation.surface: A signature is verified by two businesses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held by' signals the container; 'two companies' supplies both outer parts, one abbreviated and one a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To confirm something is to verify or authenticate it as genuine.

clue.text: Avarice shown by head of company, and folly — not a good man

indicators.note: head of means take the first letter of the word company
not means the good man's letters are taken out of the word for folly

parts.note: stupidity is folly
ST is the abbreviation for saint, a good man

explanation.surface: A company boss shows greed and foolishness, and is no saint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' signals the removal of the saint abbreviation, which leaves UPIDITY to follow the company's initial.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupidity is greed for money or possessions, a formal synonym of avarice.

clue.text: Those pups being crooked start a business

indicators.note: crooked means bent out of shape, so these letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Dishonest dog breeders open a firm selling those puppies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being crooked' rearranges THOSE PUPS.
explanation.definitionFit: To set up shop is an idiom for opening a business.

clue.text: This person in firm gets hurt

indicators.note: in means the word for this person goes inside the word for firm

parts.note: hard means firm, solid
this person is the speaker, me

explanation.surface: A member of staff gets injured at the company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the container. 'firm' looks like a company but means solid.
explanation.definitionFit: Harmed means hurt or injured, a past-participle synonym.

clue.text: Nominal message on present for former London mayor?

parts.note: a gift tag reads 'to' followed by the recipient
Ken Livingstone was the first Mayor of London

explanation.surface: A gift tag on a present addressed to a former mayor.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken Livingstone was Mayor of London from 2000 to 2008.
explanation.definitionFit: A token payment or gesture is a nominal one, small and symbolic.

clue.text: Royal command said to be confused

indicators.note: said means the word is heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: the throne stands for sovereign authority, the royal power to command

explanation.surface: A royal order is reported to be muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said' gives THROWN from the sound of THRONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Being thrown means being disconcerted or confused, in informal usage.

clue.text: Fretful, like a dog without lead

indicators.note: without lead means the first letter is removed

parts.note: bitchy means like a bitch, a female dog

explanation.surface: An anxious dog roams free without its leash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without lead' removes the first letter B from BITCHY; 'lead' looks like a dog leash.
explanation.definitionFit: Itchy can mean restless or impatient, so a fidgety, fretful person is itchy.

clue.text: The habit of a monk to be cold and solemn person?

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
an owl is proverbially wise and solemn-looking, so a solemn person may be called one

explanation.surface: A monk's habit is to be cold and serious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habit' looks like custom, but it is the garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowl is the hooded robe worn by a monk, part of a religious habit.

clue.text: Bird to relax, having eaten various bits of bread

indicators.note: having eaten means the rest word swallows the scrambled letters

parts.note: to rest is to relax

indicators.note: various bits of means the letters of bread are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A bird relaxes after eating crumbs of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'various bits of' rearranges the bread letters to DBREA, and 'having eaten' signals the container round them.
explanation.definitionFit: Redbreast is an old name for the robin, a common garden bird.

clue.text: Old prison to deny woman wanting entry

indicators.note: wanting entry means the woman letter seeks to get inside the deny word

parts.note: to negate is to deny

explanation.surface: A gatekeeper refuses to let a woman in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting entry' puts W inside NEGATE. Newgate was a notorious London prison, demolished in 1904.
explanation.definitionFit: Newgate was a historic London jail, now gone, so an old prison.

clue.text: Blonde to have boss being dragged along behind

indicators.note: behind means the boss word comes after the dragged-along word

parts.note: to tow is to drag along
a head is a boss

explanation.surface: A fair-haired woman has her boss trailing behind her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' puts the boss after the towing part; 'to have' and 'being' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A towhead is a person with very pale blond hair, like tow fibres.
